title: Checkpoint: Averages and Spread
objective: After this level you can choose the right average for a set of numbers and describe how spread out it is.
summary: Describe data with two numbers: an average that fits (mean, median or mode) and a spread (range or standard deviation). Percentiles place one value.

cards.headline: One number can't describe a crowd. Two get surprisingly close.
cards.body: An average says where the middle is. A measure of spread says how far the crowd wanders from it. This checkpoint puts Chapter 2's toolkit together.

items.label: Median
points: Best for lopsided data like income

cards.headline: Then say how spread out
cards.body: The range is the largest value minus the smallest: quick, but it hears only two values. The standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean, built from every value. On a bell curve, about 68% of values sit within one standard deviation and about 95% within two. And a percentile tells you where a single value stands: at the 90th, 90% are at or below it.

cards.fact: Before you pick an average, look for outliers.
cards.context: A value far from the rest can be a mistake to fix or a real case to keep, like Robert Wadlow at 272 cm. Either way, check it first: it can drag the mean while the median holds steady.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How to pick the right average, and why typical income calls for the median, not the mean.
Why two sets with the same average can differ, and how range and standard deviation show it.
What a bell curve looks like, and why about 68% of values sit within one standard deviation.
What a percentile says about one value, from growth charts to exam scores.

questions.prompt: Which average can describe a list of favorite pizza toppings?

options.label: The mean
The median
options.rationale: Toppings cannot be lined up from small to large.

options.label: The mode
The range
options.rationale: The range measures spread, and needs numbers.

questions.explanation: Toppings are categories, and only the mode works for categories: the most common topping.

questions.prompt: A company's pay includes a few huge executive salaries. Which average best describes a typical worker's pay?

options.label: The mean, because it includes the executives
options.rationale: Those few huge salaries pull the mean above most workers' pay.

options.label: The median, because the big salaries barely move it
The mode, because pay is a category
options.rationale: Pay is a number, and the mode may not be central.

options.label: The range, because it shows the top salary
options.rationale: The range measures spread, not a typical value.

questions.explanation: Lopsided data with a few very high values pull the mean up; the median stays with the typical worker.

questions.prompt: Two bus routes both run an average of 10 minutes late. What else do you need to compare them?

options.label: The mean again, worked out more carefully
options.rationale: The means already match; they hide the spread.

options.label: Nothing, since the same average means the same service
options.rationale: Same mean can hide very different spread.

options.label: The mode of the bus numbers
options.rationale: Bus numbers are labels; they say nothing about lateness.

options.label: A measure of spread, like the range or standard deviation

questions.explanation: The same mean can hide very different spread; one route might always be about 10 minutes late, the other all over the place.

questions.prompt: Heights within one sex are close to bell-shaped. About what share fall within two standard deviations of the mean?

options.label: About 50%
About 68%
options.rationale: That is within one standard deviation.

options.label: About 95%
Exactly 100%
options.rationale: A few values lie further out.

questions.explanation: On a bell curve, about 68% sit within one standard deviation and about 95% within two.

questions.prompt: A child is at the 75th percentile for height. What does that mean?

options.label: The child has reached 75% of their expected adult height
options.rationale: A percentile compares with other children, not with adult height.

options.label: As tall as or taller than 75% of children of the same sex and age
The child is taller than 75 of the other kids in their class
options.rationale: A percentile is a share of a reference group, not a count.

options.label: The child grew 75% faster than average this year
options.rationale: A percentile is a position, not a growth rate.

questions.explanation: Growth chart percentiles rank a child against others of the same sex and age: at the 75th, they equal or exceed 75%.
